ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: dry, itchy skin on arms and hands.
- Symptoms: onset a few days ago; localized to arms and hands; red and itchy; no fever or systemic symptoms; not yet spreading to face/trunk/legs; skin not markedly cracked as per patient; coconut butter used but did not help.
- Onset/duration: Симtoms began a few days prior to visit, after a swim  a few days ago.
- Triggers/exposures: recent swimming (possible irritant exposure); no new soaps/shampoos reported; used coconut butter recently; weather may be a factor; stress at work.
- Aggravating/relieving factors: swimming and exposure to pool water may have worsened; emollients attempted (coconut butter) with little improvement; dermatologist recommended topical steroids and emollients; antihistamines may help itch.
- Past medical history: no chronic illnesses mentioned; otherwise well.
- Medications/allergies: Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive); lactose intolerance described as an allergy history; no other medications reported.
- Family/social history: father with asthma, mother with hayfever; lives alone; non-smoker; no alcohol; works as a primary school teacher; reports high work-related stress.
- Vital signs/exam findings: no vitals recorded; examination details limited in transcript; doctor notes a dry, itchy, red rash localized to hands/arms; no fever; no systemic symptoms.
- Labs/imaging: none mentioned.
- Impression/plan discussed: likely dermatitis (dermatitis/eczema spectrum); treatment options include topical steroid cream, emollients, and over-the-counter antihistamines; avoid potential triggers; consider follow-up if not improving in a week.

I: I1. Irritant contact dermatitis – evidence: onset after swimming with involvement of exposed skin (hands/arms); dry, red, itchy skin consistent with irritant-induced dermatitis from pool/chlorine or other water/air irritants.
I2. Allergic contact dermatitis – evidence: potential exposure to pool chemicals, soaps, detergents, or coconut butter (recent use); pruritic rash could reflect an allergic mechanism.
D: D1. Xerosis/dry skin – evidence: prominent dryness with itch; weather or environmental factors suspected; could represent simple dry skin or a component of dermatitis.
I2: I2. Topical product reaction (coconut butter) – evidence: patient has been using coconut butter; could cause irritant or allergic reaction contributing to dermatitis.
A: A1. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – evidence: itch and dry skin; family history of atopy (father with asthma, mother with hayfever) supports predisposition; hands/arms can be affected in atopic dermatitis.
T: T1. Traumatic/contact irritation from rubbing or friction (occupational exposure as a teacher) – possible contributor but less likely as primary driver given distribution and acuity.
